extracted.intended_audience: public relations students and practitioners (public relations managers, department heads, and in-house or agency PR staff)
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and decision rules for organizing public relations departments, selecting PR models, structuring work vertically and horizontally, and planning/executing PR programs using systems/behavioral decision processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of PR model contingent on environment
rubrics_metrics.description: The choice of a public relations model should be contingent upon the nature of the organization’s environment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Environments range from static to dynamic; static environments can rely on press agentry and public-information models, while dynamic/complex environments require two-way asymmetric or two-way symmetric models. Use the model that provides the functions needed to cope with the specific environmental conditions (e.g., feedback, influence, control or adaptation).

rubrics_metrics.name: PR models (press agentry, public-information, two-way asymmetric, two-way symmetric)
rubrics_metrics.description: Four models of public relations are discussed: press agentry, public-information, two-way asymmetric, and two-way symmetric.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Press agentry and public-information primarily provide publicity/information about the organization; they do not provide feedback necessary to change the organization. Two-way asymmetric helps the organization control changes in the environment. Two-way symmetric helps the organization both change the environment and change itself when the environment changes. Choose models based on needs for publicity versus feedback and mutual adjustment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Static vs dynamic environments
rubrics_metrics.description: Environments can be characterized on a continuum from static (stable, routine) to dynamic (changing, complex).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In static environments organizations can behave routinely and rely on one-way PR models; in dynamic environments organizations should adopt two-way models to obtain feedback and to adapt or influence the environment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hage's indicators of complex environments
rubrics_metrics.description: Hage defines a complex environment as one with: (1) high levels of knowledge and technological sophistication; (2) greater demand for the organization’s services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these two indicators to assess whether an organization faces a complex environment (example: computer firm = complex; Board of Tea Tasters = static).

rubrics_metrics.name: Grunig's six characteristics separating static from dynamic environments
rubrics_metrics.description: Six characteristics found in research that separate static from dynamic environments: (1) Changes in technology; (2) Extent of mechanization; (3) Stability of demand for the organization’s products or services; (4) Amount of competition to produce the same products or services; (5) Degree of social and political support for the organization; (6) Growth in the knowledge that the organization uses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess each characteristic to gauge environmental dynamism. Examples provided (e.g., dramatic tech change in computers/steel; mechanized firms like assembly-line auto firms are static; shifting demand for car sizes; competition in TVs vs telephone service; changing social support pre/post Vietnam; explosion of electronics knowledge).

rubrics_metrics.name: Aldrich's levels of environmental complexity
rubrics_metrics.description: Aldrich's list of characteristics for complex vs less complex environments: (1) Richness/leanness of resources; (2) Homogeneity/heterogeneity; (3) Stability/instability; (4) Concentration/dispersion; (5) Consensus/dissensus; (6) Turbulence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these dimensions to evaluate environmental opportunities, competition, need for flexibility/innovation, geographic dispersion effects, public disagreement, and unpredictability. Examples illustrate each dimension (e.g., NIH = heterogeneous; small-town bank = stable; Kraft = dispersed).

rubrics_metrics.name: When to adopt two-way models
rubrics_metrics.description: The more complex, diverse, changeable, and antagonistic interpenetrating publics and organizations are, the more necessary it will be to have a two-way model of public relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If publics are numerous, heterogeneous, or antagonistic—or the organization must innovate or influence its environment—prioritize two-way asymmetric or symmetric models to obtain feedback and to adapt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structured vs unstructured vertical hierarchies
rubrics_metrics.description: Vertical structures distribute decision-making power; they can be relatively structured (closed-system management) or unstructured (open-system management).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structured hierarchies work best in simple/static environments and support press agentry/public-information models. Unstructured hierarchies are needed in complex/dynamic environments and support two-way asymmetric/symmetric models because they enable decentralization, autonomy, and innovation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centralization (vertical structure attribute)
rubrics_metrics.description: Centralization represents the extent to which power to make decisions is concentrated at the top of the organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A structured hierarchy is more centralized; to assess centralization ask employees how many decisions they can make on their own versus those requiring top-management approval. Decentralize to encourage innovation in complex environments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formalization (vertical structure attribute)
rubrics_metrics.description: Formalization indicates the degree to which an organization has rules, regulations, published procedures, job descriptions and penalties for role deviation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High formalization discourages innovation and suits routine work in static environments. Look for published rules, organization charts and formal procedures to determine formalization level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stratification (vertical structure attribute)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stratification means some roles are more important than others, with differential pay, prestige, and restricted communication between ranks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structured hierarchies are more stratified; destratify to encourage cross-rank communication and innovation in complex environments. Observe symbolic markers (corner offices, executive dining rooms) and communication patterns to assess stratification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizational complexity (vertical structure attribute)
rubrics_metrics.description: Complex organizations have more specialized roles, more educated and professionalized employees, specialized departments, and dispersed locations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complexity supports innovation needed in dynamic environments. Professionals demand autonomy, which links complexity to decentralization. Increase specialization and professionalization to respond to complex environments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match vertical structure to PR model and environment
rubrics_metrics.description: Structured vertical hierarchies (centralized, formalized, stratified) align with press agentry/public-information models; unstructured vertical hierarchies (decentralized, deformalized, destratified, complex) align with two-way asymmetric/symmetric models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When diagnosing a PR department, evaluate its vertical structure relative to the organization’s environment and the PR model the organization needs; mismatch (e.g., structured PR dept in complex environment) reduces effectiveness and prestige.

rubrics_metrics.name: Departmental subsystem differences in structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Organizations may structure some departments differently from others depending on the static/dynamic nature of each department’s environment and the tasks they perform.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether PR is treated as a journalistic/technical function (structured, constrained, low autonomy) or as a professional management function (decentralized, professionalized). Lack of delegation to PR often forces the department into press agentry/public-information roles, reducing prestige and budgets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Horizontal structures taxonomy (seven common models)
rubrics_metrics.description: Seven common horizontal structures for PR departments: (1) structure by publics; (2) structure by management process; (3) structure by communication technique; (4) structure by geographic region; (5) account executive system; (6) structure by organizational subsystem; (7) combination of methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each horizontal structure suits different organizational types and PR models; departments often combine methods. Use this taxonomy to design PR subunits that match the organization's environment and strategic priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure by publics (horizontal)
rubrics_metrics.description: PR department has components and middle-level managers for major groups of publics (media relations, employee relations, community relations, government relations, public affairs, financial relations, educational relations, activist publics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most common in business firms using two-way asymmetric or symmetric models. Works best with an unstructured vertical hierarchy because it concentrates on key interpenetrating systems in the environment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure by management process (horizontal)
rubrics_metrics.description: PR department components correspond to management processes such as planning, evaluation, communication, or research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Works best with decentralized/unstructured vertical hierarchies and two-way models; often appears in business firms where more people are involved in decision-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure by communication technique (horizontal)
rubrics_metrics.description: PR units correspond to major communication techniques such as press services, audiovisual production, or publications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appears most often in organizations practicing press agentry/publicity and public-information models (structured hierarchies, static environments). Also appears where dominant coalition delegates little power to PR (government, educational, nonprofit).

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure by geographic region (horizontal)
rubrics_metrics.description: PR components serve each location/region for organizations dispersed regionally, statewide, or nationally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often combined with other horizontal structures; suitable across PR models but especially advantageous when environment complexity stems from geographic dispersion (and when vertical structure is unstructured).

rubrics_metrics.name: Account executive system (horizontal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Common in PR consulting firms where different employees are assigned to serve each client; allows tailoring PR functions to client environments and structures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flexible: can provide technical help or broader PR functions, serve multiple publics, and vary vertical structure to fit clients. Use when individualized service per client/subsystem is needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure by organizational subsystem (horizontal)
rubrics_metrics.description: In-house variation of the account executive system: practitioners serve as 'account executives' for different subsystems of the organization, often as journalistic beats.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Usually appears in governmental and educational organizations and often supports press agentry/public-information functions. Suits organizations that view PR as publicity for different internal subsystems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination of horizontal methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Few organizations use only one horizontal method; they commonly combine publics, management process, geographic, or technique-based structures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design hybrid horizontal structures to meet multiple environmental and organizational needs (example: AT&T chart combining publics and management-process elements).

rubrics_metrics.name: Management decision-stage models (common PR/management process stages)
rubrics_metrics.description: Several stage models exist for decision making (examples cited): Haner & Ford (definition of objective; formulation of measures of effectiveness; generation of alternatives; evaluation; selection), Haynes/Massie/Wallace (consciousness; diagnosis/definition; search/analysis of alternatives; evaluation/selection; securing acceptance), Cutlip & Center (fact-finding/feedback; planning/programming; action/communication; evaluation), Marston RACE (research, action, communication, evaluation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These models can structure practitioner thinking or delegation. They cover similar processes but lack a single strong theoretical base; use them as templates mapped into the behavioral molecule for a unified approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behavioral molecule (throughput decision model)
rubrics_metrics.description: A systems-based behavioral molecule consists of the segments: Detect → Construct → Define → Select → Confirm → Behave → Detect (cycle continues). It describes how individuals/systems make decisions about behaviors (what to do) and how managers organize processes to produce behaviors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the molecule to plan PR behaviors and to allocate departmental roles (researchers: detect/construct; planners: construct/define; top managers: select/confirm; technicians: behave). Follow segments in order (ideally) but expect iteration. The confirm segment is critical for risk assessment (apply Murphy's law).

rubrics_metrics.name: Define segment (behavioral molecule)
rubrics_metrics.description: After formulating alternatives, managers must specify how each alternative can be put into operation (implementation details, time, cost, expected effects).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work through production/delivery methods, costs, target effects, and expected impacts on management's ideas/behavior. The define segment ends when a single plan of action is developed for each alternative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select segment (behavioral molecule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Managers make a decision to select an alternative to implement, typically choosing the one with the best chance of solving the problem; referent criteria from experience or values may be applied to eliminate options.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize referent criteria as heuristics (rules of thumb) and be aware of values-based rejections (e.g., refusing manipulative tactics). Avoid over-communication in this segment—excess information can delay decision-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confirm segment (behavioral molecule)
rubrics_metrics.description: After selection, managers confirm that the chosen alternative will work and is acceptable by thinking through what could go wrong (apply Murphy’s law).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If risks are acceptable proceed to behave; if risks are too great, return to construct or select. The confirm segment acts as a risk filter to avoid catastrophic failures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of research across the molecule segments
rubrics_metrics.description: Managers need different kinds of information/research at each segment: detect (identify PR problems), construct (research to formulate alternatives and understand publics), define (information on costs/methods/consequences), select (limited information; form referent criteria), confirm (information to validate earlier data and assess risks), behave (monitor implementation), detect (evaluative feedback).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the behavioral molecule as a Management Information System (MIS). Without relevant research, the manager’s process reduces to mere execution; different research types (exploratory, descriptive, evaluative) map to segments. Use feedback/evaluative research to close the loop.
